code.title: Test pyramid vs inverted suite: time and flake cost

followUps:
Invert it when the logic lives in the wiring rather than in functions, for example a thin UI over a backend, a microservice that mostly forwards calls, or a legacy system with no seams.

Unit tests there would mock everything and prove little, while a few integration or E2E tests exercise real behaviour. Example: a CRUD service with 3 lines of logic per endpoint gets 40 API-level tests and almost no unit tests. Judge by confidence per second, not by the shape.

Both sit beside the pyramid as cheap, targeted checks. Visual regression compares screenshots of components or pages (for example Storybook stories, 1 image per state) and catches layout and CSS bugs that DOM assertions miss. Contract tests (Pact, or OpenAPI schema checks) verify that a consumer and a provider agree on request and response shapes, replacing many slow E2E calls.

Run both on every PR, since each takes seconds to a few minutes.

Cap it with a rule: an E2E test must cover a critical user journey that cannot be checked lower down. For each new E2E test, ask what bug it catches that an integration test with MSW would not.

  • Set a budget, e.g. 15 tests and 10 minutes total.
  • Delete or push down a test when adding one over budget.
  • Track flake rate and runtime per test in CI.

Pages stay small by using API calls for setup, so each test checks one journey only.

code.title: toBe vs toEqual vs toStrictEqual rebuilt

followUps:
It copes with them without looping forever. Jest's equality tracks the pairs of objects it is already comparing, so when it meets the same pair again it treats that branch as equal and moves on.

Example: a = {n: 1}; a.self = a; and b = {n: 1}; b.self = b; are equal under toEqual. Cost is O(size of the graph), and the failure diff prints [Circular] for the loop.

Write one when the same domain check appears in many tests and the built-in matchers give a poor failure message. Examples: toBeValidEmail, toBeWithinRange(1, 5), or an a11y check.

Register it with expect.extend({ toBeEven(n) { return { pass: n % 2 === 0, message: () => `expected ${n} to be even` }; } }). Keep the message clear, because it is the thing a teammate reads at 2 a.m. Do not write one for a single use.

They let you check part of a value when some of it is unpredictable or irrelevant. expect.any(String) matches any string, expect.objectContaining({ id: 1 }) checks only some keys, and expect.arrayContaining([2]) checks some items.

expect(user).toEqual({
  id: expect.any(Number),
  name: 'Asha',
});

This stops a test from failing on a generated id or timestamp while still checking the name.

code.title: Stub, spy, mock and fake in plain code

followUps:
All three clear recorded calls, but they go progressively further. mockClear resets only mock.calls and mock.results. mockReset does that and also removes any implementation you set, so the mock returns undefined. mockRestore does a reset and also puts back the original method for spies.

Use restoreMocks: true in config so tests never leak.

Because a native ES module's exports are read-only live bindings, so jest.spyOn(mod, 'fn') cannot replace them: the namespace object is frozen or non-configurable. The code under test also calls its own local binding, not the property you replaced.

Solutions: use a module mock (vi.mock), pass the dependency in as an argument, or export an object with methods. Spying on CommonJS exports works because the exports object is mutable.

London (mockist) tests one class at a time with all collaborators replaced by mocks, working outside-in. Detroit (classicist) uses real collaborators and only fakes the awkward boundaries, working inside-out.

London gives fast, isolated tests and a clear design pressure, but it couples tests to interactions and breaks on refactors. Detroit survives refactoring better but failures are harder to locate. Most front-end teams lean Detroit with MSW at the network edge.

code.title: A fake clock and why promises escape it

followUps:
Replace the random jitter with a fixed value, then advance the fake clock in steps and check each wait. Example with delays of 1 s, 2 s and 4 s: stub Math.random to return 0, call await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(999) and assert 1 attempt, then advance 1 more ms and assert 2 attempts.

vi.spyOn(Math, 'random').mockReturnValue(0);
await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1000);
expect(fetchMock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);

Test the jitter range with a pure function instead.

It moves the fake clock's idea of "now" so Date.now() and new Date() return the new value, but it does not fire timers that were due. Example: set time to 2030-01-01 and a pending 1000 ms setTimeout still waits for the clock to advance.

So use setSystemTime to test date logic such as expiry, and advanceTimersByTime to run timers. It also does not change the real system clock or time zone.

Usually because something waits on a promise or a timer that the fake clock never advances. Examples: await sleep(1000) with faked setTimeout and no advanceTimers call, or a library that uses performance.now or nextTick you faked.

  • Advance the clock with the async variant so microtasks flush.
  • Use runOnlyPendingTimers for setInterval, since runAllTimers loops forever.
  • Do not fake timers for userEvent unless you pass advanceTimers.

code.title: Why jest.mock is hoisted: a mock registry

followUps:
Use the factory to spread the real module and override just that export. In Vitest: vi.mock('./api', async (importOriginal) => ({ ...(await importOriginal()), getUser: vi.fn() })). In Jest: jest.mock('./api', () => ({ ...jest.requireActual('./api'), getUser: jest.fn() })).

Alternatively vi.spyOn works when the module is CommonJS or exports a mutable object. Remember internal calls inside the module still use the real function.

It is the folder convention for manual mocks: put a file named like the module in a __mocks__ directory next to it, and call jest.mock('./api') to use it. For node_modules packages, a root-level __mocks__/axios.js is used automatically.

Without a file, jest.mock('./api') automocks: every export becomes a jest.fn returning undefined. Automocks save typing, but they hide the real shape, so prefer explicit factories.

Call vi.resetModules() (or jest.resetModules()) to clear the registry so the next await import() loads a fresh copy of the module, including its top-level state.

beforeEach(() => vi.resetModules());
const { count } = await import('./counter');

Needed for modules that read env vars or hold singletons at import time. Instances you imported earlier are not reset.

code.title: Route handlers vs call-by-call fetch mocking

followUps:
Make the handler wait, then assert the spinner appears before the response resolves. In the handler use await delay(100) (or a promise you resolve by hand), then expect(screen.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeVisible(), and finally await waitForElementToBeRemoved(...).

server.use(http.get('/api/items', async () => {
  await delay(100);
  return HttpResponse.json([]);
}));

A manually controlled promise is better than a real delay because it is deterministic.

A network failure means no response at all, which a browser reports as a rejected fetch (TypeError). An HTTP 500 is a valid response with a bad status, so fetch resolves and you check res.ok.

http.get('/api', () => HttpResponse.error());      // network failure
http.get('/api', () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 })); // HTTP 500

Test both, since the UI code paths (catch block vs status check) differ.

Generate them from the single source of truth instead of hand-writing them. Options: create types and handlers from the OpenAPI spec (openapi-typescript, orval, msw-auto-mock), validate fixtures against the schema in a test, and run a small contract or smoke suite against staging nightly.

Example: if the backend renames userName to name, regenerating types fails compilation in the 12 places that used the old name.

code.title: Finding elements by role and accessible name

followUps:
It walks the whole accessibility tree and computes roles and names for every element, which is much more work than a CSS selector. On a table with 5,000 cells, a role query can take seconds.

  • Narrow the search with within(container).
  • Pass { hidden: false } only when needed, since checking visibility is costly.
  • Use getByLabelText or getByText in hot spots.
  • Render smaller trees or virtualize in tests.

jsdom is not a real browser, so it cannot do layout, scrolling, CSS media queries, real focus behaviour, canvas, IntersectionObserver or real file pickers. getBoundingClientRect returns zeros, and toBeVisible only checks inline and computed styles it knows.

For those, use Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright component testing or an E2E test. Example: a sticky header or virtualized list must be tested in a real browser.

Test it through a small component that uses it, or use renderHook from RTL for hooks with no UI. Wrap with the providers it needs and use act or waitFor for async updates.

const { result } = renderHook(() => useCounter(1));
act(() => result.current.inc());
expect(result.current.count).toBe(2);

Prefer testing through a real component when the hook is only used in one place, because that checks what the user sees.

code.title: Auto-waiting locators versus stale references

followUps:
Log in once in a setup project, save the cookies and local storage with storageState, and let every test load that file, so you pay the login cost once instead of per test.

// setup: await page.context().storageState({ path: 'auth.json' });
use: { storageState: 'auth.json' }

For different roles, save one file per role. If tests change server state, use one account per worker so parallel runs do not collide. Test the login UI itself in a separate test.

Open the trace first: npx playwright show-trace gives a timeline with DOM snapshots, network calls, console logs and the failed action. Set trace: 'on-first-retry' and upload the trace as a CI artifact.

Then reproduce CI conditions: run with the same container, --workers count and --repeat-each=20. CI is usually slower and has fewer CPUs, which exposes race conditions and shared test data.

Do not mock the network for the critical journey, such as checkout against a staging backend, since the point is to prove the real system works. Do mock it for third-party services you do not control (payment, email, maps), for forcing errors such as a 500 or a slow response, and for removing randomness.

Example: keep your own API real, but use page.route('**/maps/**', route => route.fulfill(...)) to stub a map provider.

code.title: 100% coverage with weak asserts: mutation testing

followUps:
V8 coverage is collected by the JavaScript engine natively, so it is fast and needs no code rewrite, while Istanbul instruments your source with counters before running it, which is slower but gives consistent results on any runtime.

V8 can report slightly different branch counts, and used to be less accurate with transpiled code. Modern Vitest remaps V8 results through AST analysis and is close to Istanbul. Choose V8 for speed, Istanbul for exact branch parity or non-V8 runtimes.

An equivalent mutant is a change to the code that does not change its behaviour, so no test can ever fail on it. Example: changing i < n to i != n in a loop that always ends at n, or x * 1.

They inflate the surviving-mutant count and lower the mutation score unfairly. You find them by reading the code, and then exclude them with a comment or ignore rule.

Write each run's raw output (--coverage.reporter=json or lcov files) and merge them. Tools: nyc merge, Codecov or Coveralls flags, or lcov -a a.info -a b.info. Ensure both runs map to the same source paths and source maps.

For E2E you need an instrumented build (Istanbul plugin) or Playwright's V8 coverage API. Treat the merged number as a map of untested code, not a score.

code.title: Repeating a flaky test and fixing the race

followUps:
Record every test result with its commit, branch and retry count, then flag tests that both passed and failed on the same commit. A test that needed a retry to pass is flaky by definition.

  • Have CI export JUnit or JSON reports to a database.
  • Compute a flake rate per test over the last 100 runs.
  • Auto-quarantine when it exceeds, say, 2%, and open a ticket with an owner.

Playwright's report marks tests as "flaky" for you.

Only as a short-term bandage while you fix the cause, or for a known external fault you cannot control, such as a third-party sandbox that times out. Limit it to 1 or 2 retries and report the result as flaky, never as green.

Do not retry unit tests, where a failure almost always means a real bug or shared state. A retry can hide a race that also affects users.

Run new or changed tests many times before merge. For example, a CI step that runs changed test files with --repeat-each=20 (Playwright) or in a loop with shuffled order, and fails the PR if any run fails.

Add lint rules against waitForTimeout and fixed sleeps, and require fresh data per test. This catches roughly 20 to 50 percent of flakes before they reach main.

code.title: TDD case table for twoSum

followUps:
It can slow you down when the design is unclear, because tests written for a wrong guess have to be rewritten. It can also push you toward tiny steps and many mocks, and tests tied to implementation break when you refactor.

Strict red-green-refactor suits well-understood logic such as parsers, rules and bug fixes. For exploratory UI work, write a spike first and add tests once the shape settles. In an interview, 5 minutes of tests beats 15 minutes of ceremony.

Example tests pin down a few chosen inputs, while property-based tests (fast-check) generate hundreds of random inputs and check a rule that must always hold. When one fails it shrinks to the smallest failing input.

fc.assert(fc.property(fc.array(fc.integer()), a =>
  isSorted(mySort(a))));

Use examples to document intent and properties to find edge cases you did not think of, such as empty arrays or huge numbers.

Start with the cases that shape the algorithm: the happy path, then empty and single-element input, then boundaries (0, 1, max), duplicates and invalid input. These cover most bugs.

Order by risk: where would a wrong assumption cost the most? For a function over an array of 5 numbers, check the empty array first, since it often needs a different code path, and the one-element array second, because loops with n-1 bounds fail there.

code.title: Snapshot matcher with property matchers

followUps:
The key is the test's full name plus a counter, for example Cart shows total 1, and they are stored in a .snap file. Jest finds each snapshot by that name and call order within the test.

So if you add a snapshot call earlier in a test, the counters shift, and later snapshots compare against the wrong data. Renaming a test makes the old snapshot obsolete and writes a new one. Inline snapshots avoid both problems.

Visual regression compares screenshots (pixels) of the rendered UI, while a snapshot test compares serialized text such as a DOM tree. Visual tests catch CSS, spacing and font issues but need a stable environment, so use the same browser and container, and mask dynamic regions.

Tools: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot, Chromatic, Percy. Use a pixel threshold, e.g. 0.1%, to ignore anti-aliasing noise.

Treat the diff like code: read it, and ask whether each changed line is an intended behaviour change. Keep snapshots small so that a diff is under about 20 lines.

  • Reject a PR when the snapshot changes but the description does not mention why.
  • Prefer inline snapshots so the diff sits beside the test.
  • Never accept -u blindly; check the changed names first.

code.title: Jest to Vitest codemod

followUps:
Threads share memory and start faster, but code that uses native addons or process-wide state can break. Forks (child processes) give each test file a full separate process, which is slower to start but safer. Vitest defaults to forks.

Isolation per file means each file gets a fresh module registry, costing maybe 50 to 200 ms per file. You can turn it off (isolate: false) for speed if your tests do not share global state.

Use Vitest Browser Mode with a provider such as Playwright, so tests run inside real Chromium, Firefox or WebKit instead of jsdom. Configure test.browser: { enabled: true, provider: 'playwright', instances: [{ browser: 'chromium' }] }.

This gives real layout, focus and CSS. It is slower than jsdom, so keep it for component tests that need a browser and leave pure logic in node.

Measure first: run with --reporter=verbose or a profile to find the slowest files. Then run in parallel across workers or CI shards (--shard=1/4), only run tests related to changed files (--changed), and cut setup cost such as heavy global setup and unneeded real timers.

Example: a 12 minute suite split into 4 shards runs in about 3 minutes. Replace slow E2E checks with integration tests where possible.
